INTRODUCTION
RiseandShine brought this trademark suit on the
strained theory that PepsiCo’s 16-ounce fruit-flavored
energy drink “MTN DEW RISE ENERGY” is likely to
be confused with RiseandShine’s 7-ounce cans of
“RISE BREWING CO.” cold-brew coffee sold using
different labels, colors, and iconography.  Its case rests
almost entirely on both products’ use of the everyday
word “rise.”  Yet RiseandShine repeatedly
represented, including to the U.S. Patent and
Trademark Office, that third-party use of the word
“rise” made the term “extremely weak” with “little
source identifying significance that could contribute to
any likelihood of confusion.”  RiseandShine filed suit
anyway.
A district court granted a preliminary injunction,
but the Second Circuit vacated it in a scholarly opinion
by Judge Leval (joined by Judges Chin and Menashi).
On the inherent-strength subfactor of the court’s
eight-factor likelihood-of-confusion test, the panel
held that “rise” is inherently weak given, inter alia, its
strong logical associations with coffee, consistent with
RiseandShine’s prior admissions. It thus concluded
that RiseandShine’s trademark “commands a narrow
scope of protection.”  The district court subsequently
granted summary judgment to PepsiCo.  The Second
Circuit affirmed in an unpublished opinion stating
that inherent strength is a question of law.
RiseandShine hopes this Court will call inherent
strength a “question of fact,” allowing it to escape the
Second Circuit’s careful legal reasoning.  Inherent
strength, however, is quintessentially legal.  It
concerns how much exclusionary power to grant a

2


mark based on the word’s intrinsic nature.  Evaluating
inherent strength does not involve deciding historical
facts, making credibility determinations, or engaging
in other tasks indicative of factual questions.  Instead,
it requires examining the meaning of words and
balancing the scope of a trademark owner’s monopoly
power with important principles of free competition
and the First Amendment to prevent chilling speech—
all paradigmatic judicial functions.
Across intellectual property, the issue of how
broadly an IP owner can enforce rights is a legal
question.  In copyright, for example, after determining
that a work is copyrightable, courts decide the scope of
protection (e.g., whether rights are narrow or broad)
as a legal question.  In patent cases, this Court held
that determining the scope of patent rights is
exclusively within the province of courts.  Inherent
strength, which concerns the scope of trademark
protection, should be no different.
RiseandShine’s contrary argument is an exercise
in obfuscation and is designed to limit a meaningful
role for courts.  RiseandShine contends that a mark’s
inherent strength rests exclusively on its
distinctiveness—i.e., its placement on a spectrum of
classifications ranging from “generic” to “fanciful.”
RiseandShine then devotes essentially its whole brief
to arguing that distinctiveness is a question of fact
because it concerns consumer perceptions.  That
strategy fails at the threshold, because distinctiveness
and inherent strength  are separate inquiries.
Distinctiveness addresses whether a mark is  valid to
begin with, while inherent strength concerns the scope
of a valid mark’s protection—i.e., its intrinsic power to

3


exclude.  RiseandShine’s effort to collapse those two
inquiries into one makes no sense and would
effectively read inherent strength out of existence.
And apart from that attempted erasure, RiseandShine
offers no argument that inherent strength lacks the
legal element the Second Circuit rightly considered in
concluding that its mark is inherently weak.
In any event, even assuming that inherent
strength reduces entirely to distinctiveness, it still
would not be a factual question.  Courts treat similar
inquiries conducted from the consumer’s perspective
as legal questions, particularly when free-expression
principles are implicated—and, tellingly,
RiseandShine never even identifies what evidence of
consumer perception it would offer.  At the very least,
the uncontested aspects of the Second Circuit’s
reasoning warrant upholding the judgment.
A ruling that the inherent-strength component of
the judge-made likelihood-of-confusion test is a
question of law recognizes the historic difference
between classifying a mark on the spectrum of
distinctiveness and assessing its strength once
classified.  And it ensures judges have a role in
balancing the scope of trademark rights with
fundamental constitutional issues, leaving issues that
actually involve consumer perceptions (such as the
other component of the trademark-strength inquiry,
acquired strength) to the factfinder.  This Court
should affirm.

4


STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. Legal Background
1. Trademark protection
a.  Trademarks “have ancient origins” and “were
protected at common law and in equity” at the
Nation’s founding.  Matal v. Tam , 582 U.S. 218, 224
(2017).  The “principle underlying trademark
protection is that distinctive marks—words, names,
symbols, and the like—can help distinguish a
particular artisan’s goods from those of others.”  B&B
Hardware, Inc. v. Hargis Indus., Inc. , 575 U.S. 138,
142 (2015).  From its very first trademark decision,
this Court has recognized that a mark is entitled to
protection only if it is “distinctive in its original
signification, pointing to the origin of the article, or it
must have become such by association,” Del. &
Hudson Canal Co. v. Clark , 80 U.S. 311, 323 (1871);
see also Elgin Nat’l Watch Co. v. Ill. Watch Case Co. ,
179 U.S. 665, 673 (1901) (“[N]o sign or form of words
can be appropriated as a valid trademark” that does
not “point out distinctively the origin or ownership of
the articles to which it is affixed.”).
Over time, judges devised a range of
classifications to evaluate a mark’s “distinctiveness”
and thus its validity, i.e., entitlement to protection.  In
its early cases, this Court recognized these commonlaw classifications, holding that a “generic” or “merely
descriptive” mark is not “entitled to protection,” Clark,
80 U.S. at 323-24, whereas a mark that is “arbitrarily”
chosen or “fanciful” is sufficiently distinctive to
warrant protection, Hamilton-Brown Shoe Co. v. Wolf
Bros. & Co., 240 U.S. 251, 256-57 (1916).

5


In Abercrombie & Fitch Co. v. Hunting World,
Inc., 537 F.2d 4, 9-11 (2d Cir. 1976), Judge Friendly
summarized the “classic formulation” of these
common-law categories.  Two Pesos, Inc. v. Taco
Cabana, Inc. , 505 U.S. 763, 768 (1992).  In order of
“increasing distinctiveness,” they are: (1) generic,
(2) descriptive, (3) suggestive, (4) arbitrary, and
(5) fanciful.  Id.  Judge Friendly’s Abercrombie rubric
is frequently denoted the “spectrum of distinctiveness”
and is now the accepted method for determining a
mark’s validity, i.e., its entitlement to protection.  U.S.
Patent & Trademark Office v. Booking.com B.V. , 591
U.S. 549, 553 (2020).  Judge Friendly explained, for
example, that courts adopted the middle “suggestive”
category to “accord protection to marks that were
neither exactly descriptive on the one hand nor truly
fanciful on the other,” and he noted that “the validity
of a mark ends where suggestion ends and description
begins.”  Abercrombie, 537 F.2d at 10.
b.  The Lanham Act “largely codified” commonlaw trademark doctrine.  Moseley v. V Secret
Catalogue, Inc., 537 U.S. 418, 428 (2003).  To “protect
marks,” the Act established “a voluntary registration
system” administered by the U.S. Patent and
Trademark Office (PTO).  Jack Daniel’s Props., Inc. v.
VIP Prods., Inc. , 599 U.S. 140, 146 (2023).  A mark’s
registration on the “principal register” constitutes
“prima facie evidence” of the mark’s validity, among
other benefits.  Id. at 146-47; see Iancu v. Brunetti, 588
U.S. 388, 391 (2019).
Whether a mark warrants placement on the
principal register turns on its classification on the
spectrum of distinctiveness.  The Lanham Act makes

6


two categories of marks from this spectrum ineligible
for the principal register.  First, “[g]eneric terms are
not registrable.”  Park ‘N Fly, Inc. v. Dollar Park &
Fly, Inc. , 469 U.S. 189, 193-94 (1985); see 15 U.S.C.
§§1052, 1064(3).  Second, “merely descriptive” terms
are not eligible for the principal register, unless they
have “acquired distinctiveness” (or “secondary
meaning”).  15 U.S.C. §§1052(e)(1), 1052(f); Two Pesos,
505 U.S. at 769.  The PTO also cannot register a mark
that is (among other restrictions) “likely … to cause
confusion” with another mark.  15 U.S.C. §1052(d);
Matal, 582 U.S. at 227.
The Lanham Act does not mention the other three
judge-made categories on the spectrum of
distinctiveness—“suggestive,” “arbitrary,” and
“fanciful.”  This Court, however, has recognized that
marks in these three categories are “inherently
distinctive” and thus “may be placed on the principal
register.”  Booking.com, 591 U.S. at 553.  At the same
time, the Court has also repeatedly acknowledged that
a mark’s placement on the principal register, via
classification on the spectrum of distinctiveness,
pertains only to whether a mark is “eligible for
protection”; it has not opined on what determines the
amount of protection a mark receives.  Id.; see also,
e.g., Two Pesos, 505 U.S. at 768 (explaining that the
“latter three categories of marks” are “inherently
distinctive” and thus “entitled to protection”).
2. Trademark infringement
The Lanham Act “also creates a federal cause of
action for trademark infringement.”  Jack Daniel’s ,
599 U.S. at 147.  A mark owner can allege that
“another is using a mark that too closely resembles the

7


plaintiff’s.”  B&B Hardware , 575 U.S. at 144.  A
defendant is liable if the plaintiff owns a mark entitled
to protection and the defendant’s use of its own mark
“is ‘likely to cause confusion’” as to the origin,
sponsorship, or association of the defendant’s goods or
services.  Jack Daniel’s, 599 U.S. at 147; see 15 U.S.C.
§§1114(1)(a), 1125(a)(1)(A).
This Court has never addressed how to satisfy the
Lanham Act’s “likelihood of confusion” standard.
Accordingly, the courts of appeals have formulated
multi-factor tests for evaluating whether a plaintiff
established a likelihood of confusion.  The first of these
tests was articulated by Judge Friendly in Polaroid
Corp. v. Polarad Electronics Corp. , 287 F.2d 492 (2d
Cir. 1961).  He observed that “likelihood of confusion”
is a “function of many variables,” including “the
strength of [the] mark, the degree of similarity
between the two marks, the proximity of the products,
the likelihood that the prior owner will bridge the gap,
actual confusion, and the reciprocal of defendant’s
good faith in adopting its own mark, the quality of
defendant’s product, and the sophistication of the
buyers.”  Id. at 495.  Other circuits subsequently
adopted variants of the Polaroid framework.  See, e.g.,
In re Chippendales USA, Inc. , 622 F.3d 1346, 1353
n.12 (Fed. Cir. 2010) (noting the “influential ‘Polaroid
test’”); Perini Corp. v. Perini Constr., Inc. , 915 F.2d
121, 127 (4th Cir. 1990); Int’l Kennel Club of Chi., Inc.
v. Mighty Star, Inc. , 846 F.2d 1079, 1087 (7th Cir.
1988).
Consistent with Polaroid, all circuits consider
“trademark strength” as a factor.  Trademark strength
refers not to a mark’s validity or eligibility for

8


protection, but to the “scope of trademark protection
to which the mark is entitled.”  Top Brand LLC v. Cozy
Comfort Co. , 143 F.4th 1349, 1364 (Fed. Cir. 2025)
(quoting Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 406
F.3d 625, 631 (9th Cir. 2005)).  “Under the Lanham
Act, stronger marks receive greater protection.”  A&H
Sportswear, Inc. v. Victoria’s Secret Stores, Inc. , 237
F.3d 198, 222 (3d Cir. 2000).  If “[a] mark is
particularly strong, use of that mark by another can
give rise to likelihood of confusion even if the use
occurs in connection with a totally distinct product
line,” whereas “if a mark is weak, use of a similar
mark even on similar goods is unlikely to cause
confusion if minor differences distinguish one party’s
mark from another.”  Water Pik, Inc. v. Med-Sys., Inc.,
726 F.3d 1136, 1151 (10th Cir. 2013).
Courts typically divide a mark’s overall strength
into two subfactors: “inherent strength” (sometimes
called “conceptual strength”) and “acquired strength”
(sometimes called “commercial strength”).
Pet.App.51a.  This Court has never addressed, much
less defined, either subfactor, and the circuits have
adopted varying definitions, particularly as to
inherent strength.  Lower courts have defined
inherent strength as anything from “the linguistic or
graphical ‘peculiarity’ of the mark,” CareFirst of Md.,
Inc. v. First Care, P.C. , 434 F.3d 263, 269 (4th Cir.
2006), to “the obviousness of [a mark’s] connection to
the good or service to which it refers,” Network
Automation, Inc. v. Advanced Sys. Concepts, Inc. , 638
F.3d 1137, 1149 (9th Cir. 2011).  One treatise—
without citation to any case—defines it as “the
inherent potential of the term at the time of its first
use.”  J. Thomas McCarthy, McCarthy on Trademarks

9


& Unfair Competition §11:73 (5th ed. 2023)
(“McCarthy”).  The circuits are more settled on a
definition of acquired strength, which generally
means “the degree to which [a mark] has achieved
public recognition in the marketplace.”  Pet.App.51a.
B. Factual Background
RiseandShine was founded in 2015 by prep-school
classmates.  C.A.App.535-38.  Their goal was to “find
something … that would have [them] retired by forty,”
and they decided to market nitrogen-infused coldbrew coffee.  C.A.App.997-98.
The founders initially chose RISE COFFEE CO.
for the company’s trademark.  C.A.App.898.  They
explained that the word “rise” “symbolizes the start of
a new day and getting up and on the go,” and “[t]here’s
something energetic” about it.  C.A.App.977.  At the
time RiseandShine selected RISE COFFEE CO., over
twenty companies were already using “rise”-formative
marks for beverages alone, including coffee (e.g., RISE
UP COFFEE ROASTERS), as the following products
illustrate:

10



C.A.App.404-10, 490-99.
In 2015, RiseandShine attempted to register
RISE COFFEE CO. with the PTO.  C.A.App.916.  The
PTO rejected RiseandShine’s application, citing a
“likelihood of confusion with” other registered marks
for coffee products using “Rise.”  C.A.App.436-37.
RiseandShine responded, “[M]any entities have used
the word ‘Rise’ in relation to [RiseandShine’s] goods,
making it unlikely that consumers would give
significant weight to this term in ascertaining the
source of such goods.”  C.A.App.438-39.  RiseandShine
identified “at least six” registered marks “that include
the term Rise for various types of coffee goods.”  Id.
Accordingly, RiseandShine asserted, the “term ‘Rise’
is extremely weak” and has “little source identifying
significance that could contribute to any likelihood of
confusion”; furthermore, “it would be disingenuous to
claim” that marks using “Rise” “are strong.”  Id.
Instead, such marks “should be given a narrow scope
of protection” such that no company can claim broad,
exclusive rights to “Rise.”  Id.
The PTO reaffirmed the refusal.  C.A.App.214.
RiseandShine abandoned its application and
reapplied using RISE BREWING CO., which the PTO

11


registered, indicating that it found the word “brewing”
(not “rise”) sufficient to differentiate RiseandShine’s
new mark from the various other “rise” marks.
C.A.App.260, 267.  In 2016, RiseandShine launched its
coffee product, which is sold in small 7-ounce cans:

C.A.App.94, 97.
In 2018, a company using the mark RISE
BISCUITS DONUTS sent a cease-and-desist letter to
RiseandShine alleging confusion from RiseandShine’s
RISE BREWING CO. mark.  C.A.App.983.
RiseandShine responded that “claims to the RISE
mark are inherently weak,” again taking the position
that no company could broadly claim rights to “rise.”
C.A.App.989.  RiseandShine identified over 40
registered marks using the word “rise”—including for
“coffee,” “soft drinks,” and “energy drinks”—and
stated that “RISE is so commonly used … that it is
relatively weak and afforded only a narrow scope of
protection.”  C.A.App.988-91.  RiseandShine does not
mention any of these admissions in its brief.
Two years after starting RiseandShine, its
founders contacted PepsiCo about an investment or
“outright sale.”  C.A.App.111-12, 973-75.  PepsiCo
politely rebuffed RiseandShine’s outreach and
repeated follow-ups.  C.A.App.783-84, 852-54, 923,
932, 1015-16.

12


In 2020, PepsiCo began developing a fruitflavored energy drink (not a coffee drink) under its
popular Mountain Dew brand.  C.A.App.302.  PepsiCo
chose the name MTN DEW RISE ENERGY because it
evoked “morning energy and new beginnings” and the
concept of “‘rising up’ and overcoming obstacles.”
C.A.App.306, 940.
PepsiCo launched MTN DEW RISE ENERGY in
2021.  C.A.App.302-04.  It was sold in 16-ounce cans
(over double the size of RiseandShine’s cans) bearing
a lion’s head logo, the famous MTN DEW mark, and
vivid colors:

Pet.App.17a; C.A.App.302-06.
C. Procedural History
1. Preliminary-injunction proceedings
a.  In 2021, RiseandShine sued PepsiCo, alleging
Lanham Act and state-law violations.  C.A.App.220.  It
sought a preliminary injunction enjoining PepsiCo’s
mark, which the district court granted.  Pet.App.66a.
The court applied the Second Circuit’s eight-factor
Polaroid framework.  Pet.App.79a.  It determined that
the “strength of the mark” factor “tilts slightly” toward
RiseandShine because “the word ‘RISE’” is
“suggestive” and RiseandShine had provided some

13


evidence of “market distinctiveness.”  Pet.App.80a-
84a.  The court also determined that the “similarity of
the marks” factor “tips strongly” toward RiseandShine
because “the two marks are confusingly similar in
appearance.”  Pet.App.84a-86a.  The court held that
RiseandShine would likely establish likelihood of
confusion.  Pet.App.80a, 87a-91a.
b.  The Second Circuit vacated the preliminary
injunction.  Pet.App.45a-63a.  In a published opinion
by Judge Leval, joined by Judges Chin and Menashi,
the court held that the preliminary injunction was
“premised on two significant errors.”  Pet.App.46a.
First, the Second Circuit held that the district
court erred in concluding that the “strength of mark”
factor “slightly favored” RiseandShine.  As to the
mark’s inherent strength, the Second Circuit agreed
that the mark should be classified as “suggestive” on
the spectrum of distinctiveness.  Pet.App.51a, 54a.
But, the court explained, “labeling a mark as
‘suggestive’ is not the end of the inquiry,” because
“[s]uggestiveness” is “not necessarily dispositive of”
inherent strength.  Pet.App.54a.  The court observed
that “it does not necessarily follow that every
suggestive mark is stronger than every descriptive
mark.”  Pet.App.57a.
The Second Circuit held that the district court
committed “legal error” in neglecting to account for
these considerations.  Pet.App.55a.  The court added
that there is a “legal element in the determination of
how much strength a given mark commands.”
Pet.App.55a.  It faulted the district court for “fail[ing]
to note … the strong logical associations between ‘Rise’
and coffee,” which rendered the mark—while

14


suggestive as a matter of distinctiveness—“inherently
weak.”  Pet.App.57a; see Pet.App.56a (cataloguing the
“close associations between the word ‘Rise’ and coffee”
and noting that the “intended and achieved reference
of the RISE mark is illustrated by Plaintiff’s company
name—RiseandShine—something that a morning cup
of coffee helps us to do”).  The court observed, “The
trademark law does not favor giving one marketer an
exclusive right to prevent others from using such
valuable marketing terms”—like the word “rise”—“in
their own marketing campaigns.”  Pet.App.59a.
The Second Circuit also faulted the district court
for “discount[ing]” RiseandShine’s prior statements
about its mark’s inherent weakness.  Pet.App.59a.
The court noted RiseandShine’s claim to being the
“exclusive user of the principal term ‘RISE’ to identify
a single-serving, canned caffeinated beverage,” but
highlighted “over 100 uses of the term ‘Rise’ in
connection with coffee, tea, bottled beverages, energy
drinks, soft drinks, drinkable health supplements,
cafes, yogurts, and granolas”— i.e., breakfast-related
products similarly “allud[ing] to increased energy,
particularly in the morning hours.”  Pet.App.55a-56a,
58a.  The court remarked that RiseandShine had
“acknowledged [a] crowded field in its application to”
the PTO yet now “argues that there is no such room
for multiple ‘Rise’ marks to coexist peacefully, even
outside the coffee sector”—a position that was “not
persuasive.”  Pet.App.58a-59a; see also  Pet.App.63a
(explaining that RiseandShine “chose a weak mark in
a crowded field”).  The court further held that
RiseandShine had “not shown that its RISE mark has
achieved sufficient acquired strength.”  Pet.App.61a.

15


Second, the Second Circuit held that the district
court committed “clear error” in finding the marks
“confusingly similar.”  Pet.App.61a.  The court found
that neither the “shared use” of the word “rise” nor
“the use of large bold letters” rendered “the two
products ‘confusingly similar.’”  Pet.App.62a.
Moreover, it noted, the two cans “are different in size,
proportion, style, color, and artwork”; the word “RISE”
is “presented in very different manners,” with the
word on PepsiCo’s product “partially covered at the top
by [PepsiCo’s] prominently displayed house mark,
‘MTN DEW’”; the “lower half of [PepsiCo’s] can depicts
a large, stylized lion’s head” complementing “the can’s
angular font”; and RiseandShine’s “seven-ounce can is
less than half the size of [PepsiCo’s] sixteen-ounce
can,” as shown here:

Pet.App.62a-63a; C.A.App.402.  In short, there “is
little about the appearance of the two cans that would
suggest to a consumer that they come from the same
source.”  Pet.App.63a.

16


2. Summary-judgment proceedings
a.  After discovery, PepsiCo sought summary
judgment.  RiseandShine submitted no new inherentstrength or similarity evidence, and “minimal” new
acquired-strength evidence.  Pet.App.9a.  Notably, it
offered no acquired-strength or consumer-confusion
surveys, while PepsiCo submitted six surveys showing
no confusion.  Pet.App.32a, 35a-37a.
The district court granted summary judgment for
PepsiCo.  Pet.App.15a-44a.  As to inherent strength,
the court adhered to the Second Circuit’s “binding
conclusion” that the mark is “weak.”  Pet.App.28a.  As
to acquired strength, the court held that
RiseandShine’s evidence was “similar[]” to its prior
evidence and “no reasonable jury could conclude” that
RiseandShine’s mark achieved commercial strength
“linking the Rise mark to [RiseandShine’s] product.”
Pet.App.30a, 32a.  The court remarked that
RiseandShine “provide[d] no context to determine”
whether its advertising spending “is significant in the
relevant market” and “offer[ed] no survey evidence in
support of acquired meaning.”  Pet.App.32a.
As to similarity, the district court observed that
the Second Circuit had deemed its prior determination
“clear error” and “the record has not changed since”
then.  Pet.App.34a-35a.  Thus, this factor “weigh[ed]
strongly against” RiseandShine.  Id.
The district court then weighed the Polaroid
factors, noting that the “ultimate question of

Pet.App.42a.  The court concluded that RiseandShine

summary judgment for PepsiCo.  Pet.App.43a.

17

In an unpublished, unsigned summary order, the

is a legal or factual question.  Nor did it challenge any

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I.  A trademark’s inherent strength is a legal
question.  Inherent strength comprises a trademark’s
conceptual scope of protection and the intrinsic power
of a word or phrase to exclude other marks.
Determining inherent strength does not turn on
historical facts, credibility assessments, conflicting
evidence, or other customary indicia of factual
questions.  Nor does it turn on consumer perception,
which is the province of the other component of
trademark strength, acquired strength.  Rather,
evaluating a mark’s conceptual power to exclude
occurs independent of disputed facts.  Judges
routinely expound upon the meanings and

19


associations of words and phrases in statutes,
contracts, patents, and other written instruments.
There is no principled reason to exclude trademarks
and the inherent-strength inquiry from that bailiwick.
Judges are also better-positioned to address and
resolve the broader legal issues that the inherentstrength inquiry implicates.  Trademark law seeks to
balance the protection of trademark owners’ goodwill
and enhancement of consumer choice, on the one
hand, with the undesirability of allowing a monopoly
on words and phrases, on the other hand.  The
stronger a mark, the greater the mark owner’s ability
to suppress the speech of others, triggering concerns
about market competition and the First Amendment.
These competitive and constitutional concerns
reinforce not only that inherent strength is a legal
inquiry, but also that striking the right balance among
opposing public interests is properly allocated to
judges.  That is especially so given that trademarks
can last indefinitely, creating the possibility of
timeless monopolies over words and phrases, thereby
elevating the importance of a judicial role.
This Court has held that defining the scope of
other intellectual property is a legal question.  Judges
determine the scope of patent claims—an antecedent
to patent infringement—because claim construction
requires determining the meaning of words and
because judicial interpretation ensures greater
predictability and uniformity.  Patent obviousness and
subject-matter eligibility are also legal questions,
despite turning on underlying factual inquiries.
Similarly, courts also hold that whether a copyrighted
work is entitled to narrow (“thin”) or broad protection

20


is a legal question.  Determining the inherent strength
of a trademark should receive the same treatment.
II.  RiseandShine bases its contrary position on
two premises:  (1) inherent strength is equivalent to
distinctiveness ( i.e., placement of a mark on the
spectrum from generic to fanciful), and
(2) distinctiveness is a question of fact.  RiseandShine
is wrong about both premises.
First, inherent strength is not equivalent to
distinctiveness.  Distinctiveness resolves whether a
trademark is  valid —whether it is entitled to
protection in the first place.  Inherent strength
assumes a valid mark and then resolves its degree of
intrinsic power to exclude for purposes of the
likelihood-of-confusion inquiry.  It would make no
sense for those two different determinations to
collapse into one; indeed, RiseandShine’s position
effectively reads inherent strength out of existence.
That flaw is fatal to RiseandShine’s
position.  RiseandShine’s entire argument is that
inherent strength is a question of fact because
distinctiveness is a question of fact.  But because
inherent strength is not the same as distinctiveness—
and because it includes the undeniably legal
considerations that the Second Circuit invoked—
RiseandShine’s argument fails.
Second, and in any event, RiseandShine is wrong
that distinctiveness is a question of fact.  This Court
has long resolved disputes over distinctiveness on its
own, with no reference to factfinding.  RiseandShine
is also mistaken that determinations made from the
perspective of consumers are necessarily factual
questions.  The law is full of examples to the contrary,

21


particularly when a determination implicates
constitutional principles, as distinctiveness does.
RiseandShine’s remaining arguments further
undermine its position.  RiseandShine suggests that
inherent strength must be a question of fact because
likelihood of confusion is purportedly a question of
fact.  But the Second Circuit held that likelihood of
confusion is a question of law, and RiseandShine did
not seek review of that decision.  RiseandShine also
invokes the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right, but
that has nothing to do with whether a given
determination is legal or factual.  To the extent the
jury’s role is relevant, moreover, RiseandShine’s
position will inject uncertainty into trademark law by
sending more infringement cases to unpredictable
juries and making it harder to clear marks.
III.  Even if inherent strength were purely
factual, affirmance remains warranted.  First, the
Second Circuit’s reasoning and the uncontroverted
record support the conclusion that no reasonable jury
could find RiseandShine’s mark inherently strong.
Second, the Second Circuit’s uncontested rulings on
the other Polaroid factors justify summary judgment
of no likelihood of confusion.
ARGUMENT
RiseandShine asked this Court to decide whether
inherent strength is a question of law or fact.  But its
opening brief reveals that this case turns largely on a
different, logically antecedent question: what does
inherent strength include?  RiseandShine assumes
(with essentially no argument) that inherent strength
consists exclusively of placing a mark on the
distinctiveness spectrum, which it contends is a

22


factual determination.  That argument fails at its first
step.  Inherent strength is not the same as
distinctiveness.  Inherent strength includes
undeniably legal considerations that RiseandShine
does not even acknowledge, much less refute.
RiseandShine is thus wrong on the question presented
for reasons entirely separate from those that dominate
its brief.  That is all the Court needs to conclude in
order to decide (or dismiss) this case.  In any event,
RiseandShine is wrong about the principal argument
in its brief, too: even if inherent strength were
equivalent to distinctiveness, it would not be a
question of fact because distinctiveness is a question
of law.
I. A TRADEMARK’S INHERENT STRENGTH
IS A LEGAL QUESTION.
As this Court has acknowledged, “the appropriate
methodology” for distinguishing legal and factual
questions is “elusive.”  Miller v. Fenton, 474 U.S. 104,
113 (1985).  Nevertheless, the principles the Court has
applied when addressing this subject demonstrate
that the inherent-strength inquiry is a legal question.
In determining whether a question is legal or
factual, the Court has long looked to “the nature of the
inquiry itself.”  Id. at 115; see also U.S. Bank, N.A. v.
Village at Lakeridge, LLC , 583 U.S. 387, 395 (2018)
(addressing the “nature” of the question).  Although
there is no agreed-upon definition of inherent
strength, it is best understood as the intrinsic “degree
of legal muscle (or power to exclude) possessed by” a
word or phrase.  Pierre N. Leval, Trademark:
Champion of Free Speech, 27 Colum. J.L. & Arts 187,
191 (2004).  A mark inherently possessing “substantial

23


muscle”—an inherently strong mark—has the “power
to exclude not only the identical mark in the identical
area, but also confusingly similar marks in broad
areas.”  Id.  A mark that is inherently weak—even if
it “has legal validity” and is thus entitled to
protection—“can exclude others only within a very
narrow scope,” such as from “using the same mark on
the same goods.”  Id.  Assessing trademark strength
“hems in the scope” of such marks: “[t]he weaker a
mark, the fewer are the junior uses that will trigger a
likelihood of consumer confusion.”  Booking.com, 591
U.S. at 562.
The inherent-strength inquiry is, as the name
suggests, “inherent” or “conceptual.”  Unlike acquired
strength, inherent strength “looks to the mark itself,
divorced from consumers’ actual knowledge of it.”
Souza v. Exotic Island Enters., Inc. , 68 F.4th 99, 111
(2d Cir. 2023).  Inherent strength thus lacks the
customary indicia of a factual question.  It does not
turn on any “‘basic’ or ‘historical’ fact,” i.e., “who did
what, when or where, how or why.”  U.S. Bank, 583
U.S. at 395; see also Google LLC v. Oracle Am., Inc. ,
593 U.S. 1, 24 (2021) (addressing “subsidiary factual
questions” like “how much of the copyrighted work
was copied”).  It does not involve “state of mind,” “the
credibility of witnesses,” or “an evaluation of
demeanor.”  Miller, 474 U.S. at 113-14, 116-17.  There
is no “conflicting testimony” to reconcile.  Id. at 117.
Determining a mark’s inherent “power to exclude”
occurs “independent of disputed facts,” and “factual
development at trial will not change the district
court’s answer,” indicative of a “legal question.”
Dupree v. Younger, 598 U.S. 729, 737 (2023).

24


The task of determining a mark’s inherent “power
to exclude,” moreover, is well-suited for judges.  In
distinguishing between factual and legal questions,
this Court has looked to whether “one judicial actor is
better positioned than another to decide the issue in
question.”  Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc. ,
517 U.S. 370, 388 (1996).  “The construction of written
instruments” is “one of those things that judges often
do and are likely to do better than jurors.”  Id.  Courts
thus “treat document construction as a question of
law,” Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 574 U.S.
318, 325 (2015), and judges routinely expound upon
the meanings and associations of words and phrases
in statutes, contracts, patents, and other written
instruments.  See, e.g. , Loper Bright Enters. v.
Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 386 (2024); M&G Polymers
USA, LLC v. Tackett, 574 U.S. 427, 435 (2015).  There
is no reason to exclude trademarks, which likewise
involve the written word, from that bailiwick.  There
is especially no reason to exclude the inherentstrength inquiry, the entire point of which is to
examine the conceptual nature of a word and its
intrinsic power to exclude others’ use—functions
customarily performed by, and properly allocated to,
judges.
The Court’s decision in Markman is instructive.
That case addressed whether patent claim
construction is “a matter of law” or “a jury issue.”
Markman, 517 U.S. at 372, 377.  The Court explained
that “[v]ictory in an infringement suit requires a
finding that the patent claim covers the alleged
infringer’s product or process, which in turn
necessitates a determination of what the words in the
claim mean.”  Id. at 374.  And it held that determining

25


“what the words in the claim mean” was “better
suited” for “judges, not juries.”  Id. at 388; see also
Teva, 574 U.S. at 332-33 (explaining that claim
construction is “a legal question” even if “courts …
make subsidiary factual findings”).  Similarly,
determining “what the words … mean” in a trademark
and their corresponding inherent power to exclude—a
threshold step in every trademark infringement suit—
is equally “better suited” for “judges, not juries.”
Judges are also better-positioned to address and
resolve broader legal issues that the inherent-strength
inquiry implicates.  For example, trademark law has
long sought to balance the “twin goals of facilitating
consumers’ choice and protecting producers’ good
will,” Jack Daniel’s , 599 U.S. at 147, with “the
undesirability of allowing anyone to obtain a complete
monopoly” on a word as a trademark, KP Permanent
Make-Up, Inc. v. Lasting Impression I, Inc. , 543 U.S.
111, 122 (2004); see also Jack Daniel’s, 599 U.S. at 164
(Sotomayor, J., concurring) (noting “the Lanham Act’s
careful balancing of ‘the needs of merchants for
identification as the provider of goods with the needs
of society for free communication and discussion’”
(quoting Leval, supra, at 210)).  The stronger a mark,
the greater a trademark owner’s ability to prevent
others from using not just identical but nonidentical
(and increasingly dissimilar) words and phrases.  See
Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Samara Bros., Inc. , 529 U.S.
205, 210 (2000) (“Competition is deterred … not
merely by successful suit but by the plausible threat
of successful suit[.]”).  Granting an owner exclusive
rights in a mark “when there is a close conceptual
connection between the mark and the associated goods
or services” is “antithetical to trademark’s goals of fair

26


competition and consumer protection.”  Jeanne C.
Fromer, Against Secondary Meaning, 98 Notre Dame
L. Rev. 211, 214 (2022).  The “competitive advantages
associated with exclusive control of particularly
powerful words have real costs for consumers.”
Christopher Buccafusco et al., Competition and
Congestion in Trademark Law , 102 Tex. L. Rev. 437,
440 (2024).
Those same considerations, moreover, can trigger
First Amendment concerns.  To be sure, “when a
challenged trademark use functions as ‘sourceidentifying,’ trademark rights ‘play well with the First
Amendment.’”  Jack Daniel’s, 599 U.S. at 159 (quoting
Mattel, Inc. v. MCA Records, Inc. , 296 F.3d 894, 900
(9th Cir. 2002)).  But that proposition necessarily
contemplates that First Amendment concerns are
triggered when a trademark is not “sourceidentifying.”  Trademarks can also involve “expressive
value” beyond (or instead of) source identification, and
were courts “to ignore the expressive value that some
marks assume, trademark rights would grow to
encroach upon the zone protected by the First
Amendment.”  Mattel, 296 F.3d at 900; see
Scholars.Br.27-28 (explaining that “trademark law …
can be used to suppress free speech”).
These competitive and constitutional concerns
underscore the importance of ensuring that
trademarks are, in fact, “source-identifying” without
stifling competition and raising First Amendment
concerns.  And they reinforce that judges, rather than
lay juries, are best positioned to perform that inquiry.
See Bose Corp. v. Consumers Union of U.S., Inc. , 466
U.S. 485, 502 (1984) (noting that “the constitutional

27


values protected by the rule make it imperative that
judges … make sure that it is correctly applied”).  As
the leading organization of intellectual-property
owners attests, “plenary judicial determination” of
inherent strength “will ensure that free-speech rights
are respected at the same time that proper trademark
rights are enforced.”  IPO.Br.12-13.
Indeed, precisely because the determination of a
mark’s inherent strength will have an “impact on
future cases and future conduct”—by establishing the
meaning and associations of a word or phrase—the
“stakes” are “too great to entrust … to the judgment of
the trier of fact.”  Bose, 466 U.S. at 501 n.17; see Daryl
Lim, Trademark Confusion Revealed: An Empirical
Analysis, 71 Am. U. L. Rev. 1285, 1288 (2022) (noting
that “trademarks last indefinitely, meaning their
owners obtain a timeless monopoly”); Barton Beebe &
Jeanne C. Fromer, Are We Running Out of
Trademarks?, 131 Harv. L. Rev. 945, 1025 (2018)
(explaining that because “[t]hree-quarters of our word
usage consists of words registered as marks and
almost nine-tenths consists of words confusingly
similar to registered marks … we use all of our
language in the shadow of trademark rights”).
This Court, moreover, has held that defining the
scope of other intellectual property is a legal question.
As explained, for example, defining the scope of a
patent’s claims is “exclusively within the province of
the court,” Markman, 517 U.S. at 372,
notwithstanding the potential for “subsidiary factual
findings,” Teva, 574 U.S. at 332.  That is so not only
because patents are “written instruments,” but
because of “the importance of uniformity in the

28


treatment of a given patent,” without which “a ‘zone of
uncertainty’ … would discourage invention only a
little less than unequivocal foreclosure of the field.”
Markman, 517 U.S. at 390.  Similarly, the
“obviousness” of a patent is “a legal determination,”
even though “questions of fact” inform the analysis.
KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 427 (2007).
So too for the subject-matter eligibility of patents.  See
SAP Am., Inc. v. InvestPic, LLC , 898 F.3d 1161, 1166
(Fed. Cir. 2018).
Copyright law likewise treats the scope of
protection as a legal question.  In Feist Publications,
Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co. , 499 U.S. 340
(1991), this Court held that factual compilations,
while not categorically excluded from copyright
protection, are entitled to “thin” ( i.e., narrow)
protection extending only “to the particular selection
or arrangement” of facts, since facts themselves “may
not be copyrighted.”  Id. at 349-51.  Based on that
ruling, courts of appeals hold that whether a
copyrighted “work is entitled to ‘broad’ or ‘thin’
protection” is a legal question, too.  Apple Comput.,
Inc. v. Microsoft Corp. , 35 F.3d 1435, 1443 (9th Cir.
1994); see also SAS Inst., Inc. v. World Programming
Ltd., 64 F.4th 1319, 1326 (Fed. Cir. 2023) (“[T]he court
is tasked with determining the scope of copyright
protection.”).  And many circuits “hold that
copyrightability is always an issue of law” because,
although the analysis “is fact-specific,” judicial
oversight ensures that the existence and scope of
intellectual-property rights “not be placed at the
mercy of a jury.”  Gaiman v. McFarlane, 360 F.3d 644,
648-49 (7th Cir. 2004) (collecting cases).

29


In Google, this Court addressed the “‘fair use’
doctrine,” which “impose[s] limitations upon the scope
of copyright protection even [for] works that are
entitled to a copyright.”  593 U.S. at 18.  Though fair
use is “mixed” with “subsidiary factual questions”—
such as “how much of the copyrighted work was
copied”—the Court held that the “ultimate question
whether those facts showed a ‘fair use’ is a legal
question for judges to decide.”  Id. at 23-24.  In so
holding, the Court underscored that “fair use” was
“originally a concept fashioned by judges” and that the
doctrine “play[s] an important role in determining the
lawful scope of a … copyright.”  Id. at 22, 24.
Like determining the scope of a copyright or
patent, determining the scope of a trademark through
the inherent-strength inquiry is a question of law.
Akin to patent claim construction, judicial evaluation
of inherent strength maintains “uniformity in the
treatment of a given” trademark.  Markman, 517 U.S.
at 390.  Because a trademark “holder should know
what he owns, and the public should know what he
does not,” legal rulings provide necessary guidance to
market entrants.  Festo Corp. v. Shoketsu Kinzoku
Kogyo Kabushiki Co. , 535 U.S. 722, 731 (2002).  And
just as judges decide whether copyright protection is
“broad” or “thin,” or whether copyright “fair use” has
been established, so too should judges decide the
intrinsic scope of a trademark through the inherentstrength inquiry—which, like “fair use,” evolved from
judge-made doctrines.
Finally, in the same way that copyright law asks
judges to determine whether a work is “closer to the
core of intended copyright protection than others,”

30


Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569, 586
(1994), the inherent-strength inquiry ensures that
enforcement furthers the intended goals of trademark
law, including the tradeoffs between source
identification and free communication.  See Andy
Warhol Found. for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith ,
598 U.S. 508, 526-27 (2023) (explaining that
copyright’s fair-use doctrine reflects a “balancing act
between creativity and availability”).  Inherent
strength is a legal “check that can help to keep” a
trademark “monopoly within its lawful bounds.”
Google, 593 U.S. at 22.
The legal character of the inherent-strength
inquiry is confirmed by comparison to the other
component of trademark strength: acquired strength.
All agree that acquired strength is a factual question,
and understandably so, for it contains the markers of
a factual question.  Whereas inherent strength is
“divorced from consumers’ actual knowledge of” a
mark, Souza, 68 F.4th at 111— i.e., is unrelated to
consumer perception—acquired strength “evaluates
the actual customer recognition value of the mark at
the time registration is sought or at the time the mark
is asserted in litigation to prevent another’s use,”
McCarthy §11:80.  There is nothing “conceptual” about
that inquiry; it turns on “‘basic’ or ‘historical’ fact[s],”
like advertising expenditures, promotional efforts,
and other data that establish “public recognition in the
marketplace.”  Pet.App.51a; U.S. Bank , 583 U.S. at
394.  Determining whether that evidence shows
“actual customer recognition value” is a prototypical
factfinding exercise that requires no particular
expertise and implicates no broader legal concerns.
And because the inquiry turns on specific evidence

31


regarding public recognition in the marketplace at a
specific time, acquired-strength findings lack the
permanence of inherent-strength determinations,
which announce the intrinsic strength of a word or
phrase independent of circumstance.  In short, the
acquired-strength component does the “factual” work
of trademark strength, while the inherent-strength
component does the “legal” work.
II. RISEANDSHINE ERRS IN CONTENDING
THAT INHERENT STRENGTH IS A
FACTUAL QUESTION.
RiseandShine’s position on the question
presented rests on two premises.  First, RiseandShine
assumes (with essentially no argument) that a mark’s
inherent strength  turns exclusively on its
distinctiveness—i.e., its placement on the spectrum
between generic and fanciful.  Second, RiseandShine
contends that distinctiveness is a factual question.
Combining those two premises, RiseandShine
concludes that inherent strength is a factual question.
That argument fails at the threshold because
inherent strength is not equivalent to distinctiveness.
As explained above, inherent strength includes
considerations that are legal—and those
considerations were the basis for the inherentstrength determination below.  That is enough to
foreclose RiseandShine’s position on the question
presented:  because inherent strength is not limited to
distinctiveness but instead includes the legal elements
properly invoked by the Second Circuit, inherent
strength is a question of law in every respect relevant
here.  That is true regardless of whether
distinctiveness is properly regarded as a factual

32


question, and this Court therefore need not reach that
issue.  In any event, distinctiveness is a question of
law, so both of RiseandShine’s premises fail and its
position on the question presented is doubly wrong.
A. Inherent Strength Is Not Equivalent To
Distinctiveness, So It Is Irrelevant
Whether Distinctiveness Is Factual.
RiseandShine’s entire argument on the question
presented turns on the premise that inherent strength
is defined exclusively by “where the mark falls on the
distinctiveness spectrum.”  Petr.Br.6.  Thus, in
RiseandShine’s view, inherent strength is “assessed
by answering a single question: How distinctive is the
mark … along the distinctiveness spectrum, from
generic to fanciful”?  Petr.Br.13 (emphasis added); see,
e.g., Petr.Br.15 (“inherent strength … is a question of
where a mark falls along the spectrum of
distinctiveness”); Petr.Br.24 (equating the “legal
standard” for inherent strength with “the
distinctiveness spectrum”); Petr.Br.35 (same).
That premise is wrong.  Placing a mark on the
distinctiveness spectrum does not alone determine a
mark’s inherent strength.  A mark’s conceptual power
to exclude implicates the additional considerations
described above, which are legal rather than factual.
As the Second Circuit cogently explained, classifying
a mark on the spectrum does not end the inquiry;
inherent strength has an “undeniable legal element,”
which was the basis for the inherent-strength
determination in this case.  Pet.App.55a; see
Pet.App.7a.  The Court need go no further to affirm.
1. Despite RiseandShine’s attempt to conflate
them, trademark strength and distinctiveness are

33


different concepts that play different roles in
trademark law.  “[D]istinctiveness is an issue of the
trademark[’s] validity,” while “[s]trength is an issue of
infringement.”  McCarthy §11:75 (emphases in
original); see also SG.Br.4-7 (describing
distinctiveness as part of validity and inherent
strength as part of infringement).  “Keeping separate”
those concepts “is key to a coherent analysis of
trademark law questions.”  McCarthy §11:75.
Start with distinctiveness.  As explained above,
distinctiveness is the sine qua non  of trademark
protection—i.e., validity.  See pp.4-6, supra.  “If a
designation is not ‘distinctive,’ it is not a legally
protectable ‘mark.’”  McCarthy §4:13.  Distinctiveness
is thus “a yes or no issue: either a designation is
distinctive and is a valid trademark or it is not.”  Id.
§11:75; see id.  §4:13 (“No distinctiveness—no
validity—no mark.”).  This Court’s trademark
decisions from the beginning have treated
distinctiveness as relating to whether a mark is
“entitled to legal protection.”  Clark, 80 U.S. at 323;
see also  Jack Daniel’s , 599 U.S. at 146 (registration
system designed to “protect marks”); Booking.com,
591 U.S. at 553-54 (describing distinctiveness
categories “eligible for” and “ineligible for protection”);
Wal-Mart, 529 U.S. at 210; Qualitex Co. v. Jacobson
Prods. Co., 514 U.S. 159, 171 (1995); Two Pesos, 505
U.S. at 768.
To determine a mark’s distinctiveness—and thus
its validity—courts use the spectrum of classifications
crystallized by Judge Friendly in Abercrombie.  See,
e.g., Two Pesos , 505 U.S. at 768; McCarthy §11:1-2.
Under that approach, a mark is classified as either

34


generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary, or fanciful.
Two Pesos, 505 U.S. at 768-69.   A mark’s entitlement
to protection follows directly from its placement on the
spectrum.  See id.  A generic mark is never valid; a
descriptive mark is valid only if it has secondary
meaning; and a suggestive, arbitrary, or fanciful mark
is valid even without secondary meaning.  See id.; see
also, e.g., Booking.com, 591 U.S. at 553-54.
Importantly, the distinctiveness determination
does not involve any inquiry into a mark’s relative
position within a particular classification.  It does not
matter, for example, whether a suggestive mark is
closer to the border with a descriptive mark or an
arbitrary mark; if the mark is suggestive, then it is
valid—with no further questions asked.  E.g.,
McCarthy §11:75.
Trademark strength—of which inherent strength
is a component—is a different inquiry.  The strength
inquiry “assumes that there is a valid trademark  and
evaluates just how strong that trademark is” for
purposes of measuring likelihood of confusion in an
infringement claim.  Id. (emphasis added).  The
inherent-strength inquiry thus does not even begin
until the distinctiveness inquiry is complete and
validity confirmed.  That is why courts have entirely
different tests for distinctiveness ( e.g., the
Abercrombie test) and inherent strength (one
subfactor in the Polaroid test).  And that is why the
Second Circuit’s analysis of inherent strength here did
not stop with classifying RiseandShine’s mark as
“suggestive,” which was undisputed.  Pet.App.54a.
In stark contrast to distinctiveness, trademark
strength—including inherent strength—“is not a yes

or no issue.”  McCarthy §11:75 (emphasis added).  It is
instead “a question of degree,” as a mark’s strength
“can vary on a spectrum from very weak to very
strong,” regardless of the distinctiveness

is matter of degree).  So even within a particular
classification on the spectrum, courts refer to marks
as relatively weak or strong.  E.g., Variety Stores, Inc.
v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. , 888 F.3d 651, 662 (4th Cir.

suggestive, these marks are conceptually weak.”);
Brookfield Commc’ns, Inc. v. West Coast Entm’t Corp.,

“[s]ome weak marks are weaker than others”); John
H. Harland Co. v. Clarke Checks, Inc. , 711 F.2d 966,
974-75 (11th Cir. 1983) (concluding that mark is “not
particularly strong”).

errs in assuming that inherent strength can be

distinctiveness spectrum.  A distinctiveness

serves as a starting point for determining a mark’s

the mark “Booking.com” because the combination of a
generic word like “Booking” and the generic term
“.com” necessarily resulted in a mark that was generic

rejected this “nearly per se rule that would render
‘Booking.com’ ineligible for registration regardless of
the specific evidence of consumer perception.”  Id.  By

between determining a mark’s validity and
determining its protection against infringement.

that whether a mark is distinctive enough to be
registered (validity) is a different question from
whether a competitor’s use of a mark is likely to cause
confusion (infringement).  Id. at 562.  Underscoring
the separate inquiries, the Court explained that even
if a mark is valid, a similar mark will not necessarily
be found infringing.  Id.  The Booking.com markholder
even “concede[d]” that its mark, though registrable,
would be “weak” for purposes of an infringement claim

confusion.”  Id. (citations omitted).

validity and its scope of protection ensures that
trademark law fosters competition rather than
prevents it.  As this Court explained in Booking.com,
the likelihood-of-confusion inquiry for infringement

might otherwise arise from registering marks that are
not particularly distinctive.  Id.  So although a mark

B. In Any Event, Distinctiveness Is Not A
Factual Question.
Although this Court can affirm without reaching
the central argument in RiseandShine’s brief—that
distinctiveness is a question of fact—RiseandShine is
wrong on that argument, too.  Distinctiveness is a
question of law, not of fact.  Accordingly, RiseandShine
would be wrong on the question presented even if it
were somehow right that inherent strength is defined
to mean the same thing as distinctiveness.
1.  RiseandShine builds its argument that
distinctiveness is a factual question around
Booking.com and Hana Financial , but it overreads
both cases.
At the outset, Booking.com cuts heavily against
RiseandShine’s position because its analysis centered
on registration and validity, not infringement or
trademark strength.  See pp.36-38, supra.
Furthermore, Booking.com did not purport to
address—let alone resolve—whether distinctiveness
is a legal or factual question.  That was not the
question presented in the case, nor did the parties

43

RiseandShine’s position.4

either.  That case, which involved a design mark ( i.e.,

doctrine of trademark tacking presents a factual

a markholder “in limited circumstances” to “clothe a
new mark with the priority position of an older mark”
when “the original and revised marks … create the

20.  It is no surprise this Court found that the tacking

the broader considerations in the inherent-strength

While tacking simply requires a factfinder to compare
two versions of the same mark and decide whether
they present the same commercial impression,

supports that sweeping rule.  While Hana Financial

§1125(a).  Courts agree that an allegedly false

would be “received by the consumer.”  InSinkErator,

See Petr.Br.34-35; see also  SG.Br.27-30.  But the
Second Circuit squarely rejected the latter

declined to seek review of that issue.  This Court

In another distraction, RiseandShine and its

See Petr.Br.25-26; INTA.Br.20-21; AIPLA.Br.10-11.
But the Seventh Amendment has no relevance to the

resolve it without a jury.  See, e.g. , Georgia v.

strength is a factual question, it may be a question for
the jury to decide in some postures but not others—
and the difference has nothing to do with the question
presented.  For example, if a trademark-infringement
suit seeking damages proceeds to a jury trial, the jury
can resolve factual questions.  See Dairy Queen, Inc. v.
Wood, 369 U.S. 469, 479 (1962).  But if a plaintiff seeks
only equitable relief, the court must resolve factual

III. THE COURT SHOULD AFFIRM SUMMARY
JUDGMENT FOR PEPSICO REGARDLESS.
Even if inherent strength were purely factual,
affirmance for PepsiCo remains warranted on two
grounds.  First, the Second Circuit’s decision supports
the conclusion that no reasonable jury could find that
“rise” is inherently strong.  Second, the other Polaroid
factors and the unchallenged aspects of the decisions
below support summary judgment of no likelihood of
confusion.  See, e.g., Monasky v. Taglieri, 589 U.S. 68,
85-86 (2020) (affirming rather than vacating after
correcting lower court’s standard); Global-Tech
Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. , 563 U.S. 754, 770-71
(2011) (same).

52


A. The Second Circuit’s Reasoning
Supports The Conclusion That No
Reasonable Jury Could Find
RiseandShine’s Mark Inherently Strong.
RiseandShine acknowledges that if inherent
strength is a factual issue, summary judgment may
still be appropriate.  Indeed, RiseandShine concedes
that Hana Financial allowed for summary judgment
in the consumer-perception context.  See Petr.Br.32-
33; accord SG.Br.30-32.  Should the Court hold that
inherent strength is factual, affirmance remains
warranted because the Second Circuit’s analysis
supports the conclusion that no reasonable jury could
find that “rise” is inherently strong.  See CVSG.Br.19
(Government’s invitation brief stating the Second
Circuit’s reasoning “may simply reflect the … view
that no reasonable factfinder could have found
RiseandShine’s mark to be inherently strong”).
The uncontroverted record and the reasoning of
the published opinion amply support that conclusion.
While acknowledging RiseandShine’s claim to being
the only “single-serving canned caffeinated beverage”
using “‘RISE’ as the principal term”—a
gerrymandered description RiseandShine repeats
here, see Petr.Br.3—the Second Circuit nevertheless
described, inter alia, (i) “the strong logical associations
between ‘Rise’ and coffee”; (ii) the “direct[]” connection
between “[t]he word ‘Rise’” and “energy itself”; and
(iii) the “over 100 uses of the term ‘Rise’ in connection
with coffee, tea, bottled beverages, energy drinks” and
other breakfast-related products “allud[ing] to
increased energy, particularly in the morning hours.”
Pet.App.56a, 58a.  The court also noted

53


RiseandShine’s founders’ acknowledgment that “Rise”
“symbolizes the start of a new day and getting up and
on the go” and being “energetic”— i.e., its ordinary
meaning—and that they even named their company
after a phrase connoting the same.  C.A.App.977;
Pet.App.56a.  The Second Circuit further highlighted
RiseandShine’s prior acknowledgment to the PTO
that the “term ‘Rise’ is extremely weak” and should
receive “a narrow scope of protection,” Pet.App.57a-
58a, an admission RiseandShine reiterated in
defending against a potential infringement claim, see
pp.10-11, supra.  RiseandShine cannot leverage the
inherent weakness of “Rise” in selecting and defending
its trademark, yet then assert that “Rise” is inherently
strong when seeking to prevent others from using the
word.
Notably, RiseandShine has never identified any
“evidence of consumer perception” (including
consumer surveys) regarding the inherent strength of
“rise,” Petr.Br.32—much less evidence creating a
genuine factual dispute that consumers consider “rise”
inherently strong.  If anything, that telling omission
reinforces that inherent strength is a legal question.
At a minimum, it shows that no reasonable jury could
find “rise” strong, as the Second Circuit’s decision
supports.
B. The Other Polaroid Factors Support
Summary Judgment For PepsiCo
Regardless.
Even assuming a genuine factual dispute on
inherent strength, summary judgment of no likelihood
of confusion remains appropriate given the Second

54


Circuit’s unchallenged determinations regarding the
other Polaroid factors.
For one, the Second Circuit held that
RiseandShine had not “raised triable issues of fact
regarding the acquired strength of its mark.”
Pet.App.8a.  RiseandShine cites advertising
expenditures and other branding efforts.  Petr.Br.3,
10.  But the Second Circuit “agree[d] with the district
court” that such evidence did not create a genuine
factual dispute, “especially in the absence of any
consumer studies that link the ‘RISE’ mark to
RiseandShine,” which is “probative” in the Second
Circuit.  Pet.App.8a-9a; see Centaur Commc’ns, Ltd. v.
A/S/M Commc’ns, Inc., 830 F.2d 1217, 1223 (2d Cir.
1987) (“[The] test of secondary meaning is not the size
of the expenditure used to create it but its
effectiveness[.]”).  RiseandShine does not challenge
those determinations in this Court.
For another, in granting summary judgment, the
district court held that the “similarity” factor “weighs
strongly against” RiseandShine.  Pet.App.34a-35a.
RiseandShine did not appeal that ruling, and the
Second Circuit’s decision affirming summary
judgment reiterated that RiseandShine’s mark “does
not resemble PepsiCo’s mark.”  Pet.App.12a.  The
Second Circuit also noted that, under circuit
precedent, the “similarity-of-marks factor” is
“dispositive … when the marks are sufficiently
dissimilar.”  Pet.App.12a.  RiseandShine does not
contest that precedent here, or the Second Circuit’s
determination that its mark “does not resemble

55


PepsiCo’s mark,” thus rendering this factor
“dispositive” under Second Circuit law.6
There is more.  RiseandShine cites a “pattern” of
“actual customer confusion,” another Polaroid factor.
Petr.Br.4, 10.  But the Second Circuit held that
RiseandShine’s evidence “centered on the perceptions
of industry professionals,” thereby doing “little to
show likelihood of consumer confusion,” and that
RiseandShine “failed” to “provid[e] consumer surveys”
demonstrating “that consumers were confused.”
Pet.App.12a-13a.  Again, RiseandShine does not
dispute those determinations.  And while
RiseandShine suggests bad faith (another Polaroid
factor) because PepsiCo supposedly “admired”
RiseandShine and “considered acquiring” it, Petr.Br.3,
RiseandShine cites no evidence regarding the former
and the Second Circuit rejected the latter, stating in
yet another uncontested observation that
RiseandShine “sought a ‘partnership’ with PepsiCo,
which PepsiCo declined,” Pet.App.13a; see p.11, supra.
In short, even if RiseandShine could raise a
genuine factual dispute on inherent strength, the
Second Circuit’s unchallenged conclusions regarding
the other Polaroid factors justify summary judgment
of no likelihood of confusion.  Affirmance of the Second
